## The finding

Epic 6202's story **S1 (`aa40-cbda`, "Isolate review-gate scratch on a dedicated EBS volume") is
CLOSED, but its deliverable is not in effect.** The volume exists, is attached, and is raw and
unmounted; gate scratch is running on the ROOT filesystem, which is precisely the silent fallback
S1 exists to prevent.

## Measured on the live host, 2026-09-05 (SSM, read-only)

```
lsblk
  nvme1n1   50G  xfs   /var/gerrit   vol06fa2e77a9dd97527
  nvme0n1   60G        (root)        vol0270fcf13709cf472
  nvme2n1   50G  ----   ----         vol06780b8557d1416b7   <- NO FSTYPE, NO MOUNTPOINT

blkid /dev/nvme2n1            -> none            (no filesystem at all)
/etc/fstab                    -> entries for /, /boot/efi, /var/gerrit ONLY; no gate-scratch line
du -sh /var/lib/rebar/gate-scratch -> 9.3G       ON ROOT, actively written (mtime within 2 min)
ls -A  /var/lib/rebar/gate-scratch -> rebar-gate-snapshots, reviewbot-nopn30zv,
                                      reviewbot-t8kxn0i8, semgrep-mcp
df -h /                       -> 34G used of 60G (57%)
.gate-scratch-required        -> ABSENT
.gate-scratch-mounted         -> ABSENT
```

AWS confirms the volume is `in-use`, attached to `i-00880b2c7f13527c5` at `/dev/sdg`, and the NVMe
serial on `nvme2n1` is exactly `vol06780b8557d1416b7`. So there is no ambiguity about which device
it is — it simply was never formatted or mounted.

## Why it happened

The volume was created by a `terraform apply` **after** the instance's first boot. `user_data.sh`
runs under cloud-init on FIRST BOOT ONLY, so its `mount_ebs_volume "${gate_scratch_volume_id}"`
step has never executed for this volume. Nothing else on the host mounts it. This is a real gap in
the delivery path, not a bug in `user_data.sh`'s logic: the script is correct and simply never ran.

## The monitoring worked -- and is worth crediting

Both alarms are correctly in ALARM. `rebar-gate-scratch-unmounted` reads `gate_scratch_mounted`
= 0. `rebar-gate-scratch-disk-high` publishes NOTHING (there is no mount to `df`) and, because
`treat_missing_data = "breaching"`, alarms rather than reading healthy -- the dead-man-correct
behaviour `bff5-9163` was closed for. So this WAS detectable and detected. What was missing is
that S1 closed on code correctness without a check that the volume entered service.

## Why the marker design means this is DEGRADED, not BROKEN

`user_data.sh:236-238` places two markers on deliberately different filesystems (`chmod 0700`
at `:236`, the declaration at `:237`, the proof at `:238`; the contract is spelled out in the
comment at `:222-228`). The line range this ticket first cited, `:123-130`, is the
device-resolution `readlink -f` branch from bug `ad8d` F5 and has nothing to do with markers:
`.gate-scratch-required` beside the mount point on ROOT (the declaration), `.gate-scratch-mounted`
inside the mount point on the VOLUME (the proof). Declaration present + proof absent makes gate
admission REFUSE rather than quietly repopulate on root.

Here **both** are absent, so admission does not refuse — gates run on root. That is the degraded
path, and it has evidently been running for days. It is stable, which is why this is not a p1: root
is at 57% with 26G free. But it means the isolation S1 bought is not being had, and a gate run that
fills root now takes Gerrit down with it — the exact coupling S1 removed on paper.

## Remediation is NOT a simple mount — read this before acting

`/var/lib/rebar/gate-scratch` currently holds **9.3G of live, in-use working directories**
(`reviewbot-*` sandboxes, gate snapshots, semgrep state). Mounting the volume over that path HIDES
those contents from any process that opens them afterwards, while leaving the 9.3G stranded on root.
Doing it while a gate or review is mid-run would break that run.

The contents are genuinely scratch, so no data migration is needed — but a QUIET WINDOW is, and the
stranded copy must be removed afterwards or the space is lost twice. Sequence:

The full ordered procedure -- quiesce, MOVE the contents aside (never mount over them), format,
fstab-by-UUID, mount, assert `mountpoint -q` BEFORE any marker, write the markers proof-first,
recreate the review-bot container, reclaim, then confirm from CloudWatch -- now lives in
`infra/runbooks/gate-scratch-mount.md`, with a verification and a rollback per step. Do not
improvise from this summary.


Deliberately NOT executed tonight: seven agent sessions are pushing changes and the review-bot is
actively reviewing them, so there is no quiet window, and the degraded state is stable.

## Scope split: what lands in code, and what only an operator can do

AC1-AC4 are HOST actions on a running production box (format, mount, markers, reclaim). No agent
performs them, so they are tagged `[non-codebase]` and are discharged by an operator executing
`infra/runbooks/gate-scratch-mount.md` and recording the result here. What lands as code is that
runbook plus AC5's delivery-gap assertion. Splitting it this way is not a descope: a turnkey,
verified, rollback-per-step procedure IS the deliverable for AC1-AC4, because the risky part is
the sequence, not the individual commands.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] [non-codebase] The gate-scratch volume is formatted, in `/etc/fstab` by UUID, and mounted at
      `/var/lib/rebar/gate-scratch`. Proven by `mountpoint -q` and `lsblk` showing the fstype.
- [ ] [non-codebase] Both markers exist on their intended filesystems, created in the safe order, and
      `chmod 0700` is applied. Proven by `ls` plus confirming they are on different devices.
- [ ] [non-codebase] `rebar/host:gate_scratch_mounted` publishes 1 and `disk_used_percent` resumes publishing;
      both alarms return to OK. Proven from CloudWatch, not from the host alone.
- [ ] [non-codebase] The stranded copy under root is reclaimed and `df /` reflects it.
- [ ] AC5 (the only NON-`[non-codebase]` criterion). Concrete edit target:
      **`scripts/assert_volumes_in_service.py`** (new), with its offline oracle
      `tests/unit/test_assert_volumes_in_service_dcc3.py` (new) and an invocation section in
      `infra/runbooks/gate-scratch-mount.md`. It joins the two halves nobody had joined —
      terraform's `aws_volume_attachment` set (which volumes are attached) against the host's
      mount table (which mount points are backed by a real filesystem) — and fails, naming the
      volume, when a volume is attached but not in service. Three outcomes, not two: `UNKNOWN`
      (the host did not report the device) is distinct from `NOT-IN-SERVICE` and also fails.
      A post-boot AUTO-RECONCILER is deliberately NOT the chosen branch: auto-mounting a
      formatted volume would be safe, but this volume was RAW, and auto-`mkfs` on a volume that
      merely looks blank is how a restored backup is destroyed — so the unsafe half is exactly
      the half that was needed. Flipping `rebar.llm.gate_admission` to refuse when the
      declaration marker is absent is a real design change (it would refuse every gate on this
      box while the volume is still unmounted) and is filed separately as
      `reportable-commutual-rooster` (`1064-8c4a-f399-41de`).
- [ ] [non-codebase] The review-bot container is RECREATED after the host mount, and the mount is
      verified FROM INSIDE it. `infra/compose/docker-compose.yml:305` binds `/var/lib/rebar` —
      the PARENT — and Docker binds default to `rprivate` propagation, so a mount created on the
      host underneath a running container does NOT appear inside it. Without this the bot keeps
      writing to the shadowed pre-mount directory while every host-side check reads healthy.
      Proven by `docker compose exec review-bot sh -c 'stat -c %D /var/lib/rebar/gate-scratch;
      stat -c %D /var/lib/rebar'` returning TWO DIFFERENT device ids, and by
      `.gate-scratch-mounted` being visible inside the container.
- [ ] [non-codebase] The DELIVERY GAP is closed, not just this instance: a volume added by `terraform apply` after
      first boot is either mounted by something that runs post-boot, or its absence is made a
      loud, actionable signal at apply time. A fix that only mounts this one volume by hand leaves
      the next one to be discovered the same way — by an alarm, days later.
